claim: Impairments in metacognition are common in patients with psychiatric disorders.
source: Impairments in metacognition, the ability to accurately report one's performance, are common in patients with psychiatric disorders, where a putative neuromodulatory dysregulation provides the rationale for pharmacological interventions.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about psychiatric disorders and references to prior literature on metacognitive impairments in psychiatric populations.

claim: Unexpected arousal modulates metacognition.
source: Previously, we have shown how unexpected arousal modulates metacognition (Allen et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study by Allen et al., 2016.

claim: Noradrenergic blockade with 40 mg propranolol significantly increased metacognitive performance (type-II area under the curve, AUROC2).
source: Signal theoretic analysis of a global motion discrimination task with adaptive performance staircasing revealed that noradrenergic blockade (40 mg propranolol) significantly increased metacognitive performance (type-II area under the curve, AUROC2), but had no impact on perceptual decision making performance.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from signal detection theoretic analysis of the task performance.

claim: Noradrenergic blockade with 40 mg propranolol had no impact on perceptual decision making performance.
source: Signal theoretic analysis of a global motion discrimination task with adaptive performance staircasing revealed that noradrenergic blockade (40 mg propranolol) significantly increased metacognitive performance (type-II area under the curve, AUROC2), but had no impact on perceptual decision making performance.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing no significant differences in perceptual performance measures.

claim: Blockade of dopamine D2/3 receptors with 400 mg amisulpride had no effect on metacognition.
source: Blockade of dopamine D2/3 receptors (400 mg amisulpride) had no effect on either metacognition or perceptual decision making.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing no significant differences in metacognitive measures.

claim: Blockade of dopamine D2/3 receptors with 400 mg amisulpride had no effect on perceptual decision making.
source: Blockade of dopamine D2/3 receptors (400 mg amisulpride) had no effect on either metacognition or perceptual decision making.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing no significant differences in perceptual performance measures.

claim: This is the first study to show a pharmacological enhancement of metacognitive performance in the absence of any effect on perceptual decision making.
source: Our study is the first to show a pharmacological enhancement of metacognitive performance, in the absence of any effect on perceptual decision making.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' interpretation of their findings in the context of existing literature.

claim: Noradrenergic neurotransmission has a regulatory role in perceptual metacognition.
source: This enhancement points to a regulatory role for noradrenergic neurotransmission in perceptual metacognition.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental findings showing that noradrenergic blockade enhances metacognition.

claim: Each of the three experimental groups consisted of 20 subjects matched for gender, age, affect, and intellectual abilities.
source: Each of the three groups consisted of 20 subjects matched for gender, age, affect (Watson et al., 1988), and intellectual abilities (Wechsler, 1999) (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental design and data presented in Table 1.

claim: The dopamine group received 400 mg of amisulpride 110 min prior to the metacognition task.
source: The dopamine group received 400 mg of amisulpride (selective D2/3 antagonist) 110 min prior to a metacognition task and an additional placebo 30 min after the amisulpride administration (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental procedure as shown in the text and Figure 1A.

claim: The noradrenaline group received 40 mg of propranolol 80 min prior to the task.
source: The noradrenaline group received a placebo at 110 min prior to the task and then 40 mg of propranolol (non-selective β-adrenoceptor antagonist) 30 min after placebo administration.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental procedure for drug administration timing.

claim: Subjects were not aware of whether and which drug they received.
source: A post-experiment evaluation revealed that subjects were not aware of whether and which drug they received (χ2(4)=1.26, p=0.868; missing data from two subjects).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of post-experiment evaluation data.

claim: There were no effects of drug on mood ratings.
source: There were no effects of drug on mood (PANAS; Watson et al., 1988) ratings (main effect of drug: F(2,57)=.16, p=0.852; time x drug: F(2,57)=.19, p=0.827; time x affect x drug: F(2,57)=2.17, p=0.124).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of PANAS mood ratings showing no significant differences.

claim: Subjects performed a visual global motion discrimination task that included confidence judgements.
source: Eighty minutes after the second drug administration, subjects performed a visual global motion discrimination task that included confidence judgements (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental task as shown in the text and Figure 1B.

claim: Subjects decided whether the overall motion of a short burst of randomly moving dots was directed to the left or right of the vertex.
source: Subjects decided whether the overall motion of a short burst of randomly moving dots was directed to the left or right of the vertex.
evidence: This claim describes the perceptual task used in the experiment.

claim: Subjects indicated confidence in their decision using a sliding visual analogue scale.
source: Subsequently, and in the absence of feedback on whether they were correct or not, they indicated confidence in their decision on that trial using a sliding visual analogue scale.
evidence: This claim describes the method for measuring metacognitive judgements.

claim: A staircase procedure was used to match subjects' decision accuracy and control for potential drug effects on perceptual performance.
source: To control for potential drug effects on perceptual performance, we matched the subjects' decision accuracy by continuously adapting the global motion orientation using a staircase procedure (Cornsweet, 1962).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design feature to control for performance differences, supported by citation to the staircase method.

claim: Type-II performance measures subjects' awareness into their own performance by assessing how well their confidence ratings match their true accuracy.
source: This measures subjects' awareness into their own performance by assessing how well their confidence ratings match their true accuracy (i.e., 'how much more confident am I if I make a correct vs incorrect decision').
evidence: This claim defines the metacognitive measure used, based on signal detection theory.

claim: There was a significant effect of drug on AUROC2 (F(2,55)=5.192, p=0.009, η²=0.16).
source: The analysis revealed a significant effect of drug on AUROC2 (Figure 2, F(2,55)=5.192, p=0.009, η²=0.16), with follow up t-tests showing the propranolol group performed significantly better than a placebo group (t(38)=4.00, p<0.001, d = 1.26).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the metacognitive performance data.

claim: The propranolol group performed significantly better than the placebo group on AUROC2 (t(38)=4.00, p<0.001, d = 1.26).
source: The analysis revealed a significant effect of drug on AUROC2 (Figure 2, F(2,55)=5.192, p=0.009, η²=0.16), with follow up t-tests showing the propranolol group performed significantly better than a placebo group (t(38)=4.00, p<0.001, d = 1.26).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis comparing the two groups.

claim: The propranolol group performed marginally better than the amisulpride group on AUROC2 (t(36)=2.02, p=0.051, d = 0.65).
source: The propranolol group also performed marginally better than an amisulpride group (t(36)=2.02, p=0.051, d = 0.65) with the latter having an equal performance as the placebo group (t(36)=.74, p=0.465, d = 0.23).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis comparing the two groups.

claim: The amisulpride group had equal AUROC2 performance as the placebo group (t(36)=.74, p=0.465, d = 0.23).
source: The propranolol group also performed marginally better than an amisulpride group (t(36)=2.02, p=0.051, d = 0.65) with the latter having an equal performance as the placebo group (t(36)=.74, p=0.465, d = 0.23).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no significant difference between groups.

claim: A Bayesian two-sample t-test comparing placebo and amisulpride groups revealed a Bayes Factor of 3.31, corresponding to moderate evidence for the null hypothesis.
source: This analysis revealed a Bayes Factor of 3.31, corresponding to moderate evidence for the null hypothesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by Bayesian statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Inhibition of noradrenergic function improves metacognitive insight.
source: These results indicate that inhibition of noradrenergic function improves metacognitive insight, in the absence of any effect of amisulpride.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental findings showing enhanced metacognition with propranolol.

claim: There was a significant group-by-correctness interaction for confidence ratings (F(1,38)=8.66, p=0.006, η²=0.19).
source: A significant group-by-correctness interaction (F(1,38)=8.66, p=0.006, η²=0.19) in the absence of a group main effect (F(1,38)=1.83, p=0.185, η²=0.05) suggests that a confidence rating difference between correct and incorrect trials underlies the observed group differences.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of confidence ratings.

claim: The metacognitive enhancement effect was primarily driven by error trials (t(38)=2.17, p=0.036, d = 0.69).
source: Subsequent t-tests demonstrated that this effect was primarily driven by error trials (error trials: t(38)=2.17, p=0.036, d = 0.69, correct trials: t(38)=-.193, p=0.848, d = 0.06), suggesting that the propranolol group exhibited lower confidence for error trials.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis comparing confidence ratings on error versus correct trials.

claim: The propranolol group exhibited lower confidence for error trials.
source: Subsequent t-tests demonstrated that this effect was primarily driven by error trials (error trials: t(38)=2.17, p=0.036, d = 0.69, correct trials: t(38)=-.193, p=0.848, d = 0.06), suggesting that the propranolol group exhibited lower confidence for error trials.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the statistical analysis showing lower confidence on error trials in the propranolol group.

claim: Metacognitive measures can be influenced by differences in perceptual performance.
source: Metacognitive measures, as used here, can be influenced by differences in perceptual performance (Fleming and Lau, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Fleming and Lau, 2014.

claim: There was no significant difference in mean accuracy between groups (F(2,55)=1.60, p=0.212, η²=0.05).
source: We deliberately used a staircase procedure to keep performance equivalent between groups (mean accuracy: F(2,55)=1.60, p=0.212, η²=0.05, cf. Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of accuracy data.

claim: There were no significant differences in perceptual sensitivity d' between groups (F(2,55)=1.69, p=0.194, η²=0.07).
source: A signal-detection theoretic analysis confirmed these findings, revealing the absence of any significant differences in either perceptual sensitivity d' (Figure 3C, F(2,55)=1.69, p=0.194, η²=0.07) or response bias c (F(2,55)=2.29, p=0.112, η²=0.08) (Green and Swets, 1966).
evidence: This claim is supported by signal detection theory analysis of perceptual performance.

claim: There were no significant differences in response bias c between groups (F(2,55)=2.29, p=0.112, η²=0.08).
source: A signal-detection theoretic analysis confirmed these findings, revealing the absence of any significant differences in either perceptual sensitivity d' (Figure 3C, F(2,55)=1.69, p=0.194, η²=0.07) or response bias c (F(2,55)=2.29, p=0.112, η²=0.08) (Green and Swets, 1966).
evidence: This claim is supported by signal detection theory analysis of response bias.

claim: AUROC2 group differences remained after controlling for d', response bias c, and stimulus signal strength (F(2,51)=4.99, p=0.010, η²=0.17).
source: To additionally ensure that differences in AUROC2 were not influenced by any of these measures, we also compared AUROC2 using an ANCOVA with d', response bias c, and stimulus signal strength (mean orientation) as covariates, revealing the same group difference for AUROC2 after controlling for these potential biases (F(2,51)=4.99, p=0.010, η²=0.17).
evidence: This claim is supported by ANCOVA statistical analysis controlling for potential confounds.

claim: There was no significant difference in stimulus strength (mean stimulus motion orientation) between groups (F(2,55)=1.16, p=0.321, η²=0.04).
source: There was no significant difference in stimulus strength (Figure 3A, F(2,55)=1.16, p=0.321, η²=0.04), indicating perceptual performance was not significantly affected by the drug manipulations.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of stimulus parameters.

claim: Perceptual performance was not significantly affected by the drug manipulations.
source: There was no significant difference in stimulus strength (Figure 3A, F(2,55)=1.16, p=0.321, η²=0.04), indicating perceptual performance was not significantly affected by the drug manipulations.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the lack of significant differences in stimulus strength and other performance measures.

claim: There was no drug effect on reaction times (F(2,55)=.87, p=0.424, η²=0.03).
source: Likewise, there was no drug effect on reaction times (Figure 3B, F(2,55)=.87, p=0.424, η²=0.03).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of reaction time data.

claim: There was no difference in median confidence ratings between groups (F(2,55)=.38, p=0.684, η²=0.01).
source: Lastly, to test whether there were baseline differences in how the groups were utilising the confidence scale, we examined the median confidence ratings, but found no difference (Figure 3D, F(2,55)=.38, p=0.684, η²=0.01), supporting the result that an enhanced metacognitive ability under propranolol is not due to a bias in use of the confidence rating scale.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of median confidence ratings.

claim: Enhanced metacognitive ability under propranolol is not due to a bias in use of the confidence rating scale.
source: Lastly, to test whether there were baseline differences in how the groups were utilising the confidence scale, we examined the median confidence ratings, but found no difference (Figure 3D, F(2,55)=.38, p=0.684, η²=0.01), supporting the result that an enhanced metacognitive ability under propranolol is not due to a bias in use of the confidence rating scale.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the lack of differences in median confidence ratings between groups.

claim: Confidence determines how much we trust our decisions and how strongly they influence future behaviour.
source: Confidence determines how much we trust our decisions and how strongly they influence future behaviour.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about the role of confidence in decision-making.

claim: A read out of confidence in a decision that fails to reflect actual performance will lead to poor decisions and long-term adverse outcomes.
source: A read out of confidence in a decision that fails to reflect actual performance will lead to poor decisions and long-term adverse outcomes.
evidence: This claim is based on logical inference about the consequences of poor metacognition.

claim: Impaired metacognition is reported in psychiatric disorders.
source: Impaired metacognition is reported in psychiatric disorders (Frith, 1992; Knouse et al., 2005; Lysaker et al., 2010; Wells, 2011; Hauser et al., 2017), and its pharmacological remediation could provide a target for treatment (Wells, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies reporting metacognitive impairments in psychiatric disorders.

claim: Pharmacological remediation of metacognition could provide a target for treatment of psychiatric disorders.
source: Impaired metacognition is reported in psychiatric disorders (Frith, 1992; Knouse et al., 2005; Lysaker et al., 2010; Wells, 2011; Hauser et al., 2017), and its pharmacological remediation could provide a target for treatment (Wells, 2011).
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the potential therapeutic implications of the findings and supported by citation.

claim: Inhibition of central noradrenaline function enhances perceptual metacognitive ability.
source: Here we show that inhibition of central noradrenaline (by means of propranolol) function enhances perceptual metacognitive ability.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data showing enhanced AUROC2 with propranolol.

claim: Dopamine blockade had no impact on metacognition.
source: A dopamine blockade (by means of amisulpride) had no impact on metacognition and neither drug manipulation had an impact on core perceptual performance.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data showing no significant differences in AUROC2 with amisulpride.

claim: Neither drug manipulation had an impact on core perceptual performance.
source: A dopamine blockade (by means of amisulpride) had no impact on metacognition and neither drug manipulation had an impact on core perceptual performance.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data showing no significant differences in perceptual measures.

claim: Noradrenaline is known to impact arousal and higher-order cognition.
source: Noradrenaline is known to impact arousal and higher-order cognition, but the precise mechanisms remain obscure.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about noradrenaline function.

claim: The precise mechanisms by which noradrenaline impacts arousal and higher-order cognition remain obscure.
source: Noradrenaline is known to impact arousal and higher-order cognition, but the precise mechanisms remain obscure.
evidence: This claim acknowledges the current state of scientific knowledge about noradrenaline mechanisms.

claim: Influential accounts propose noradrenergic modulation of information processing through neural gain.
source: Influential accounts propose noradrenergic modulation of information processing, either through neural gain (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; Eldar et al., 2013) or by signalling unexpected uncertainty (Yu and Dayan, 2005; Dayan et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical accounts of noradrenaline function.

claim: Influential accounts propose noradrenaline signals unexpected uncertainty.
source: Influential accounts propose noradrenergic modulation of information processing, either through neural gain (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; Eldar et al., 2013) or by signalling unexpected uncertainty (Yu and Dayan, 2005; Dayan et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical accounts of noradrenaline function.

claim: Metacognition can be thought of as a higher-order process that follows a perceptual decision making stage and integrates perceptual and other sources of information to form an overall confidence judgement.
source: Metacognition can be thought of as a higher-order process that follows a perceptual decision making stage and integrates perceptual and other sources of information, such as interoceptive states and general arousal (Allen et al., 2016), to form an overall confidence judgement.
evidence: This claim is based on theoretical understanding of metacognition and supported by citation.

claim: The neural gain hypothesis proposes that noradrenaline amplifies strong and diminishes weak signals throughout the brain.
source: The neural gain hypothesis (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; Eldar et al., 2013) proposes that noradrenaline amplifies strong and diminishes weak signals throughout the brain, with the effect of an increased 'contrast' between strong and weak signals.
evidence: This claim describes a theoretical account supported by citations.

claim: Due to nonlinearity in neural gain amplification, noradrenaline is likely to neglect subtle signal differences.
source: Due to a nonlinearity in this amplification it is likely to neglect subtle signal differences, and thus omit the breath and detail of information conveyed.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the neural gain hypothesis and its implications.

claim: Noradrenaline might render detailed stimulus properties unavailable to the metacognitive process, impairing the precision of a metacognitive judgement.
source: This in turn means noradrenaline might render detailed stimulus properties unavailable to the metacognitive process, impairing the precision of a metacognitive judgement.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the neural gain hypothesis.

claim: Phasic noradrenaline is elicited by unexpected uncertainty or arousal, such as when making an erroneous choice.
source: The latter theory (Dayan et al., 2006) suggests phasic noradrenaline is elicited by unexpected uncertainty or arousal, such as when making an erroneous choice (Ullsperger et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical and empirical work on noradrenaline function.

claim: Phasic noradrenaline burst acts by interrupting ongoing processes and leads to a resetting and erasure of currently maintained information to enable an orienting response.
source: This phasic burst acts by interrupting ongoing processes and leads to a resetting and erasure of currently maintained information to enable an orienting response (Sokolov et al., 2002; Dayan et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical accounts of phasic noradrenaline function.

claim: Following an incorrect response, accumulated sensory information is reset and unavailable for confidence judgement, leading to poorer metacognitive performance.
source: In the context of our paradigm, this suggests that following an incorrect response accumulated sensory information is reset and unavailable for confidence judgement, leading to poorer metacognitive performance.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the theoretical account applied to the experimental paradigm.

claim: The primary drug-effect on confidence in erroneous trials supports the information resetting hypothesis.
source: This is supported by our finding of a primary drug-effect on confidence in erroneous trials.
evidence: This claim connects the experimental findings to the theoretical interpretation.

claim: A blockade of noradrenaline by propranolol hinders the noradrenaline-related loss of information to provide complete perceptual information to a confidence-related process.
source: On both accounts, a blockade of noradrenaline by propranolol hinders the noradrenaline-related loss of information to provide complete perceptual information to a confidence-related process.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the theoretical accounts and experimental findings.

claim: Unexpected arousal biases metacognition, an effect possibly modulated by noradrenaline.
source: This is also in line with our previous findings showing that unexpected arousal biases metacognition (Allen et al., 2016), an effect possibly modulated by noradrenaline.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work and speculation about the mechanism.

claim: Both noradrenaline and dopamine are often ascribed similar functions including a role in exploration.
source: This is of interest as both neuromodulators are often ascribed similar functions including a role in exploration (Hauser et al., 2016), neural gain (Eldar et al., 2013; Fiore et al., 2016; Hauser et al., 2016), salience (Bromberg-Martin et al., 2010; Kahnt and Tobler, 2013), (prediction) error signalling (Holroyd and Coles, 2002; Hauser et al., 2014) and effort processing (Bouret et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on neuromodulator functions.

claim: Neural recordings from dopaminergic and noradrenergic brainstem nuclei have revealed surprisingly similar neural response patterns.
source: Likewise, neural recordings from dopaminergic and noradrenergic brainstem nuclei have revealed surprisingly similar neural response patterns (Bouret et al., 2012; Varazzani et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to neural recording studies.

claim: Enhanced perceptual metacognition with noradrenaline blockade might reflect a rare sensitivity to the actions of one of these neuromodulators.
source: Our finding of enhanced perceptual metacognition with noradrenaline blockade might reflect a rare sensitivity to the actions of one of these neuromodulators.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on interpretation of the findings in the context of neuromodulator similarities.

claim: A recent report of increased performance and confidence ratings following dopaminergic enhancement may reflect a performance, but not a metacognitive, effect.
source: Our findings also raise the possibility that a recent report of increased performance and confidence ratings following dopaminergic enhancement (Lou et al., 2011) may reflect a performance, but not a metacognitive, effect.
evidence: This claim is speculative, reinterpreting previous findings in light of the current results.

claim: A previous report showed specific testosterone effects on perceptual performance but not metacognition.
source: This finding is akin to a previous report of specific testosterone effects, where there was an effect on perceptual performance but not metacognition (Wright et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study showing dissociable effects.

claim: Little is known about the precise pharmacokinetics and how comparable the dosage effects of amisulpride and propranolol are.
source: An important caveat for comparing the amisulpride and propranolol groups directly is that little is known about the precise pharmacokinetics and how comparable the dosage effects are.
evidence: This claim acknowledges limitations in the current state of knowledge about drug pharmacokinetics.

claim: Amisulpride was administered 30 min before propranolol because of slightly different absorption rates.
source: First, because of the slightly different absorption rates, we administered amisulpride 30 min before propranolol, in keeping with previous drug schedules (Peretti et al., 1997; Ramaekers et al., 1999; Strange et al., 2003; Silver et al., 2004; Strange and Dolan, 2004; Hurlemann et al., 2005; Alexander et al., 2007; Gibbs et al., 2007; De Martino et al., 2008; Kahnt et al., 2015; Kahnt and Tobler, 2017).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design rationale, supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The dosages of 40 mg propranolol and 400 mg amisulpride were selected based on previous studies of neurocognition.
source: Second, to render the cognitive effects of the drugs as similar as possible, we selected dosages that were commonly reported in previous studies of neurocognition (i.e. 40 mg propranolol, 400 mg amisulpride) (e.g., Ramaekers et al., 1999; Strange et al., 2003; Silver et al., 2004; Strange and Dolan, 2004; Hurlemann et al., 2005; Alexander et al., 2007; Gibbs et al., 2007; De Martino et al., 2008; Kahnt et al., 2015; Kahnt and Tobler, 2017).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design rationale, supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A single-dose of 400 mg sulpiride leads to an occupancy of ~28% of D2 receptors.
source: A previous study of sulpiride, which has a similar chemical formulation to amisulpride, but slightly different pharmacokinetics, suggests that a single-dose of 400 mg leads to a occupancy of ~28% of D2 receptors (Mehta et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a PET study on sulpiride.

claim: There are no PET studies reporting on single-dose amisulpride.
source: Unfortunately, there are no PET studies reporting on single-dose amisulpride, and there are no occupancy studies of propranolol, thus rendering it difficult to directly quantify and compare our dosage effects.
evidence: This claim acknowledges a gap in the existing literature.

claim: There are no occupancy studies of propranolol.
source: Unfortunately, there are no PET studies reporting on single-dose amisulpride, and there are no occupancy studies of propranolol, thus rendering it difficult to directly quantify and compare our dosage effects.
evidence: This claim acknowledges a gap in the existing literature.

claim: Noradrenaline specifically influences perceptual metacognition but not perceptual decision making.
source: In this study, we show that noradrenaline specifically influences perceptual metacognition but not perceptual decision making.
evidence: This claim summarizes the main finding of the study, supported by the experimental data.

claim: Metacognitive ability is relatively stable across different perceptual decision making tasks.
source: Recent studies show that a metacognitive ability is relatively stable across different perceptual decision making tasks (Song et al., 2011; McCurdy et al., 2013), even when probing different sensory modalities (de Gardelle et al., 2016; Garfinkel et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on metacognitive stability across tasks.

claim: It is unclear whether metacognition within different cognitive domains rely on the same processes.
source: However, it is unclear whether metacognition within different cognitive domains (e.g., perception vs memory) rely on the same processes, with evidence from neuroimaging suggesting that these functions utilise unique neural networks (Baird et al., 2013; Fleming et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim acknowledges uncertainty in the field, supported by citations to neuroimaging studies.

claim: Noradrenaline modulates activity on a whole-brain level.
source: Given that noradrenaline modulates activity on a whole-brain level (Hauser et al., 2016), it is possible that noradrenergic metacognition effects can be observed in domains other than perception, an interesting area for future studies.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a study on noradrenaline's brain-wide effects.

claim: It is possible that noradrenergic metacognition effects can be observed in domains other than perception.
source: Given that noradrenaline modulates activity on a whole-brain level (Hauser et al., 2016), it is possible that noradrenergic metacognition effects can be observed in domains other than perception, an interesting area for future studies.
evidence: This claim is speculative, suggesting directions for future research.

claim: Confidence is reflected by cardiac and pupil responses.
source: Lastly, our previous findings of an embodied reflection of confidence by means of cardiac and pupil responses (Allen et al., 2016) raise the question as to whether the observed noradrenaline effects are purely a consequence of central changes, or whether peripheral effects of this drug influence metacognitive performance independently.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous findings on embodied confidence.

claim: It is unclear whether the observed noradrenaline effects are purely a consequence of central changes, or whether peripheral effects influence metacognitive performance independently.
source: Lastly, our previous findings of an embodied reflection of confidence by means of cardiac and pupil responses (Allen et al., 2016) raise the question as to whether the observed noradrenaline effects are purely a consequence of central changes, or whether peripheral effects of this drug influence metacognitive performance independently.
evidence: This claim raises a question about the mechanism of the observed effects.

claim: A drug that exclusively targets peripheral, but not central, noradrenaline could provide insight into visceral contributions to metacognition.
source: A drug that exclusively targets peripheral, but not central, noradrenaline (cf. De Martino et al., 2008) could provide insight into the question of visceral contributions to metacognition as suggested in ideas on embodied cognition (Allen and Friston, 2016).
evidence: This claim is speculative, suggesting a future experimental approach supported by citations.

claim: Noradrenaline has a controlling influence on metacognitive ability.
source: In conclusion, using a double-blind, placebo-controlled drug manipulation we show that noradrenaline has a controlling influence on metacognitive ability.
evidence: This claim summarizes the main conclusion of the study, supported by the experimental data.

claim: Metacognition is enhanced following a blockade of noradrenergic β-adrenoceptors.
source: Metacognition is enhanced following a blockade of noradrenergic β-adrenoceptors an observation suggesting potential remedial avenues for metacognitive insight deficits seen in psychiatric patients.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data showing enhanced AUROC2 with propranolol.

claim: The findings suggest potential remedial avenues for metacognitive insight deficits seen in psychiatric patients.
source: Metacognition is enhanced following a blockade of noradrenergic β-adrenoceptors an observation suggesting potential remedial avenues for metacognitive insight deficits seen in psychiatric patients.
evidence: This claim is speculative, suggesting potential clinical applications of the findings.

claim: Sixty subjects participated in the study.
source: Sixty subjects participated in this double-blind, placebo-controlled, between-subjects study.
evidence: This claim describes the sample size of the study.

claim: Each subject was randomly allocated to one of three drug groups, controlling for an equal gender balance in all groups.
source: Each subject was randomly allocated to one of three drug groups, controlling for an equal gender balance in all groups.
evidence: This claim describes the randomization procedure used in the study.

claim: Candidate subjects with a history of neurological or psychiatric disorders, current health issues, regular medications (except contraceptives), or prior allergic reactions to drugs were excluded from the study.
source: Candidate subjects with a history of neurological or psychiatric disorders, current health issues, regular medications (except contraceptives), or prior allergic reactions to drugs were excluded from the study.
evidence: This claim describes the exclusion criteria for the study.

claim: Subjects had normal or corrected-to-normal vision.
source: Subjects had normal or corrected-to-normal vision.
evidence: This claim describes an inclusion criterion for the study.

claim: The study was approved by the UCL research ethics committee.
source: The study was approved by the UCL research ethics committee and all subjects gave written informed consent.
evidence: This claim describes the ethical approval for the study.

claim: All subjects gave written informed consent.
source: The study was approved by the UCL research ethics committee and all subjects gave written informed consent.
evidence: This claim describes the consent procedure for the study.

claim: Propranolol is a non-selective β-adrenoceptor antagonist.
source: To attenuate noradrenergic function we administered 40 mg of propranolol, a non-selective β-adrenoceptor antagonist.
evidence: This claim describes the pharmacological properties of propranolol based on established knowledge.

claim: Amisulpride is a selective D2/3 antagonist.
source: To attenuate dopamine function we administered 400 mg of amisulpride, a selective D2/3 antagonist.
evidence: This claim describes the pharmacological properties of amisulpride based on established knowledge.

claim: These drugs were chosen because of their selective high affinity effects on either noradrenaline or dopamine.
source: These drugs were chosen because of their selective high affinity effects on either one or the other of these two neuromodulators, enabling a specific dissociation of their contribution to metacognitive ability.
evidence: This claim describes the rationale for drug selection based on their pharmacological properties.

claim: The task was performed 80 min after the second drug administration.
source: The task was performed 80 min after the second drug administration.
evidence: This claim describes the timing of the experimental task.

claim: The motion stimulus was presented for 250 ms.
source: On every trial, subjects viewed a brief burst of motion (250 ms), followed by a forced choice to determine if the overall motion direction was to the left or right of vertical.
evidence: This claim describes a parameter of the experimental task.

claim: Subjects had up to 1500 ms to make their motion choice.
source: Subjects had up to 1500 ms to make their motion choice, and 2500 ms to report their confidence.
evidence: This claim describes a timing parameter of the experimental task.

claim: Subjects had 2500 ms to report their confidence.
source: Subjects had up to 1500 ms to make their motion choice, and 2500 ms to report their confidence.
evidence: This claim describes a timing parameter of the experimental task.

claim: Subjects first completed a short training session of 140 detection-only trials to establish motion thresholds.
source: Subjects first completed a short training session of 140 detection-only trials to establish motion thresholds.
evidence: This claim describes the training procedure used in the study.

claim: All subjects achieved staircase stabilization before continuing to the main experiment.
source: All subjects achieved staircase stabilization before continuing to the main experiment (the motion direction threshold reached in the final staircase of training was used as the starting point for main task).
evidence: This claim describes a criterion for proceeding to the main task.

claim: On each trial subjects viewed a cloud of 1100 moving black dots.
source: On each trial subjects viewed a cloud of 1100 moving black dots of 0.08 degrees visual angle (DVA), presented for 250 ms within a 15.69 DVA circular array at random starting positions and advancing at a speed of 0.06 DVA per frame.
evidence: This claim describes the stimulus parameters used in the task.

claim: All dots had a randomized limited lifetime of maximum 93% (14 frames) to prevent fixation on local motion directions.
source: To prevent fixation on local motion directions, all dots had a randomized limited lifetime of maximum 93% (14 frames).
evidence: This claim describes a design feature of the stimulus to control for local motion cues.

claim: Two separate staircase conditions were deployed with a fixed motion variance equal to either 20 or 30 degrees standard deviation.
source: To render the staircase opaque to subjects, and maximize confidence variability, we deployed two separate staircase conditions with a fixed motion variance equal to either 20 or 30 degrees standard deviation.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design to maximize confidence variability.

claim: Subjects completed a total of 144 trials divided evenly between four blocks.
source: Subjects completed a total of 144 trials (72 high variance, 72 low variance) divided evenly between four blocks.
evidence: This claim describes the number of trials in the main experiment.

claim: Two outlier subjects who performed worse than the rest were excluded (both belonged to the amisulpride group).
source: To ensure homogeneous performance across all subjects, we excluded two outlier subjects who performed worse than the rest (as measured using boxplots; both subjects belonged to the amisulpride group).
evidence: This claim describes the exclusion criteria applied during data analysis.

claim: All trials from the first block were omitted to ensure staircase stabilisation.
source: We omitted all trials from the first block to ensure staircase stabilisation, similar to previous studies (Fleming et al., 2010, 2012; Allen et al., 2017; Hauser et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim describes the data preprocessing procedure, supported by citations to similar approaches in previous studies.

claim: Trials with early (<100 ms), late (>1500 ms) or missing responses were excluded.
source: Trials with early (<100 ms), late (>1500 ms) or missing responses were excluded.
evidence: This claim describes the trial exclusion criteria used in data analysis.

claim: Low and high variance trials were collapsed, leaving a total of 108 trials per subject.
source: We collapsed low and high variance trials, leaving a total of 108 trials per subject, per recommended procedures, for optimal estimation of SDT measures (Fleming and Lau, 2014).
evidence: This claim describes the data analysis procedure, supported by citation to recommended practices.

claim: AUROC2 is unbiased by a subject's overall level of confidence if detection performance is held constant across subjects.
source: In contrast to classical measures of metacognition (e.g., the correlation of confidence and accuracy), AUROC2 is unbiased by a subject's overall level of confidence (or metacognitive bias/criterion) if detection performance is held constant across subjects (Fleming and Lau, 2014).
evidence: This claim describes a property of the AUROC2 metric, supported by citation.

claim: AUROC2 is not susceptible to issues such as non-normal confidence distributions.
source: Further, being nonparametric, AUROC2 is not susceptible to issues such as non-normal confidence distributions.
evidence: This claim describes an advantage of the AUROC2 metric based on its nonparametric nature.
